content: In middle-income countries, the median annual cost of generic fixed-dose formulations containing dolutegravir (DTG) or efavirenz (EFV) is comparable, ranging from $75 to $80 per person. However, with economies of scale, the price of DTG could potentially decrease to $17–$21 per person annually, which is lower than the current cost of first-line antiretroviral therapy (ART) regimens. A review of 12 studies evaluating the cost-effectiveness, cost utility, or cost savings of DTG as a first-line ART for adults concluded that DTG-based regimens are highly cost-effective compared to standard care. For children, the cost and cost-effectiveness of DTG and raltegravir (RAL) formulations remain unclear. These formulations are not widely available and are still undergoing national registration. Currently, only the originator company manufactures DTG and RAL formulations for children, but negotiated access prices are comparable to other recommended antiretroviral drugs, representing good value given the relatively low demand. The Guideline Development Group, with input from the WHO Department of Global Health Ethics, discussed the equity implications of providing DTG. They agreed that offering DTG to all individuals who can safely use it is the most equitable approach. However, given safety concerns, providing an alternative effective regimen, such as EFV 600 mg, would also be equitable. WHO conducted surveys among people living with HIV, healthcare workers, and HIV program managers to assess the acceptability, feasibility, values, and preferences regarding large-scale implementation of DTG-containing regimens. The majority of respondents preferred DTG-based regimens as first-line ART for treatment-naïve individuals (63% of people living with HIV, 79% of healthcare workers, and 75% of program managers). However, these surveys were conducted before recent data on potential safety concerns related to DTG use during the periconception period became available. When asked about preferred ART regimens while taking rifampicin for tuberculosis (TB) treatment, one-third of people living with HIV preferred once-daily EFV, while 42% preferred a twice-daily DTG-containing regimen. Among healthcare workers and program managers, 58% and 40%, respectively, favored the twice-daily DTG option for individuals co-infected with TB and HIV. Following reports of a potential association between DTG use during the periconception period and neural tube defects, a pilot survey of women living with HIV in sub-Saharan Africa was conducted. Of the 51 respondents, 75% were younger than 45 years. When asked which ART regimen WHO should recommend as first-line, 53% preferred a DTG-containing regimen, 20% preferred an EFV-containing regimen, and the rest were uncertain. Responses were divided on whether women and adolescent girls starting ART should begin with a DTG-containing regimen, with 37% answering no, 37% answering yes, and 20% uncertain. Similarly, when asked whether pregnant women starting ART should use DTG, 37% said yes, 31% said no, and 24% were uncertain. When asked how they would feel if their healthcare provider advised them to use DTG only with reliable contraception due to potential risks, 57% of women stated they would prefer to receive information and make their own decision, 22% said they would follow their provider's advice, and 20% said they would not take DTG. Concerns about safety issues related to DTG use among women and adolescent girls of childbearing potential could exclude a significant portion of the population from using DTG-based regimens, particularly in settings with high rates of unintended pregnancies and HIV prevalence, such as sub-Saharan Africa, where 60–70% of people living with HIV are women or adolescent girls. In this region, only 36% of women of childbearing age have effective access to contraception. Surveys are ongoing to assess the implementation considerations of using DTG during the periconception period, which is challenging to identify precisely. The Guideline Development Group emphasized the need for programs to provide women and adolescent girls with information, choice, and a person-centered approach to using DTG safely. Women living with HIV have expressed the need for accessible, affordable, and integrated sexual and reproductive health services. Many reported negative experiences with contraceptive choice, including being coerced into using long-acting or permanent methods or being told they could only use condoms. Some women reported that access to other services, such as safe abortion or ART, was conditional on their contraceptive use. Only about half of the women surveyed received practical support for safe conception or achieving their fertility goals. Experiences of violence were also reported as barriers to optimal sexual and reproductive health outcomes. Nearly 60% of respondents had experienced an unplanned pregnancy, and only 40% had accessed family planning services. Participants highlighted a lack of understanding and education about sexuality, pregnancy, and prevention, particularly among young women, adolescents, and key populations such as sex workers. Gender dynamics significantly influence decision-making around contraception and family planning. Women living with HIV emphasized the importance of compassionate, holistic, and informed care that respects their rights and choices, particularly regarding pregnancy, fertility, and healthy sexuality. They called for the normalization of pregnancy and childbirth among women living with HIV within health services and communities. Following the DTG safety alert, women living with HIV have advocated for the right to make informed decisions about their ART and contraception, emphasizing the need for safe, non-judgmental, and comprehensive sexual and reproductive healthcare. This includes support for adherence and managing potential side effects, regardless of their choices. Adolescent girls and women of childbearing potential face unique challenges in accessing modern contraception and preventing unintended pregnancies. In 2016, an estimated 21 million girls aged 15–19 years and 2 million girls younger than 15 years in developing regions became pregnant, with approximately half of these pregnancies being unintended. Member States have committed to ensuring universal access to sexual and reproductive healthcare services as part of the Sustainable Development Goals. Policy decisions on DTG use for adolescent girls and women of childbearing potential should prompt a review of access to sexual and reproductive health services for people living with HIV and assess the integration of these services in lowand middle-income countries. DTG-based regimens are particularly beneficial for adolescents due to their higher risk of suboptimal adherence and challenges with central nervous system side effects associated with EFV. DTG's high genetic barrier to resistance is especially important in populations at higher risk of treatment failure. Promoting the safe use of DTG in this population requires a differentiated, adolescent-friendly approach to integrated sexual and reproductive health and HIV services. These services should address barriers to access and adherence, including social and economic factors. In early 2018, approximately 500,000 people globally were using DTG, with two-thirds in high-income countries. Several lowand middle-income countries, including Botswana, Brazil, and Kenya, have adopted DTG as a preferred first-line option. By the end of 2017, nearly 70 lowand middle-income countries had included or planned to include DTG in their national guidelines. Multiple suppliers are capable of manufacturing DTG, and no capacity shortfalls are expected. Introducing DTG-based regimens for children older than six years appears feasible, particularly with simplified dosing approaches. However, treating neonates requires early infant diagnosis and linkage to care within the first four weeks of life. The use of RAL granules has been demonstrated to be feasible in low-resource settings, provided adequate training is given to healthcare workers and caregivers. A phased implementation approach is recommended, with sufficient buffer stocks of existing and new regimens maintained throughout the transition period.
